senses.gloss: Too pleased with yourself, in a way that annoys other people.
examples: He gave a *self-satisfied* smile when the numbers came in.
She looked *self-satisfied* after winning the argument.
The whole article is smug and *self-satisfied*.

senses.gloss: Where customers serve themselves instead of being served.
examples: We stopped at a *self-service* gas station outside Reno.
The cafeteria is *self-service*, so grab a tray.
*Self-service* checkout lanes move faster at this hour.

senses.gloss: Done to help yourself, while pretending to help others.
examples: His apology sounded *self-serving*.
It was a *self-serving* decision dressed up as generosity.
Nothing is *more self-serving* than helping only when the cameras are on.

position: attributive only — never after a verb
contrast: Always doubtful: the speaker gives the title because the person claims it, not because it is earned.

senses.gloss: Using a title or description that you gave yourself.
examples: A *self-styled* expert took over the meeting.
He is a *self-styled* reformer with no record to show for it.
The *self-styled* king of late-night radio signed off for good.

senses.gloss: Able to provide everything you need without help from outside.
examples: The farm is almost *self-sufficient* in vegetables.
She learned to be *self-sufficient* at a young age.
The country is *more self-sufficient* in energy than it was ten years ago.

senses.gloss: Able to keep itself going without outside help or money.
examples: The project is *self-sustaining* now and needs no more grants.
A *self-sustaining* chain reaction starts in a fraction of a second.
Her garden is small but *self-sustaining*.

senses.gloss: Caring only about yourself and not about other people.
examples: Don't be *selfish* — share the cookies with your sister.
It was a *selfish* thing to do, and he knew it.
He gets *more selfish* the longer he lives alone.

senses.gloss: Thinking about other people's needs before your own.
examples: Her years of work with refugees were entirely *selfless*.
It was a *selfless* act of courage.
The nurses did the *most selfless* work of anyone that winter.

contrast: *Semantics* is the noun: *it's just semantics* means the argument is about words, not about facts.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the meaning of words.
examples: The difference is purely *semantic*.
They spent an hour on a *semantic* detail.
*Semantic* analysis of the contract turned up two readings.

contrast: American dictionaries prefer *semiformal*, with no hyphen; the two spellings are the same word.

senses.gloss: Less formal than a black-tie event, but dressier than everyday clothes.
examples: The invitation says *semi-formal*, so wear a jacket.
It was a *semi-formal* dinner at the club.
We kept the tone of the meeting *semi-formal*.

contrast: *Semiannual* means twice a year, like *biannual*; *biennial* means every two years.

senses.gloss: Happening twice a year.
examples: The *semiannual* report comes out in June and December.
The store runs a *semiannual* sale on coats.
She goes in for a *semiannual* checkup.

senses.gloss: Partly automatic: one action by the operator, the rest by the machine.
examples: A *semiautomatic* rifle fires one round per trigger pull.
The press is *semiautomatic*: you load it and it does the rest.
*Semiautomatic* transmissions were rare on American cars.

senses.gloss: Shaped like half a circle.
examples: The seats form a *semicircular* row around the stage.
A *semicircular* window sits above the front door.
The driveway in front of the house is *semicircular*.

contrast: The usual American spelling; *semi-formal* with a hyphen is the same word.

senses.gloss: Dressier than everyday clothes, but short of black tie.
examples: He wore a *semiformal* suit to the reception.
The wedding is *semiformal* — no jeans.
*Semiformal* attire means a dark suit or a cocktail dress.

contrast: Not a *semi-* word: *seminal* comes from *seed* and means first and influential, not half of anything.

senses.gloss: Early and so important that later work grows out of it.
examples: Her *seminal* paper changed the whole field.
That record is a *seminal* album of early punk.
The book is one of the *seminal* works of the period.

senses.gloss: Lasting a long time but not forever.
examples: She uses a *semipermanent* hair color that washes out in a month.
The trailers became *semipermanent* housing for the crew.
*Semipermanent* makeup lasts about a year.

senses.gloss: Of a stone: valuable, but less so than a diamond or a ruby.
examples: The ring is set with *semiprecious* stones.
Amethyst is a *semiprecious* gem.
She keeps a tray of *semiprecious* beads for her jewelry.

senses.gloss: Slightly sweet: less sugar than sweet chocolate or wine, more than bitter.
examples: The recipe calls for a cup of *semisweet* chocolate chips.
We ordered a *semisweet* white wine.
This chocolate is *semisweet*, not bitter.

contrast: Always capitalized. *Semitic* names a family of languages and peoples; *anti-Semitic* is used only of hostility toward Jews.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the group of peoples and languages that includes Hebrew and Arabic.
examples: Hebrew and Arabic are *Semitic* languages.
The inscription is written in a *Semitic* script.
The course covers the *Semitic* peoples of the ancient Near East.

senses.gloss: Having to do with a senator or the Senate.
examples: He announced his *senatorial* campaign in the spring.
*Senatorial* courtesy decides which judges get a hearing.
A *senatorial* district in this state covers everything.

contrast: The same word is the noun, and it does not change in the plural: *a Senegalese*, *the Senegalese*.

senses.gloss: From Senegal, or having to do with Senegal.
examples: A *Senegalese* restaurant opened on Main Street.
The *Senegalese* team won on penalties.
Her mother is *Senegalese*.

contrast: Offensive about a person today — doctors say *has dementia*. The word survives in the fixed term *senile dementia*.

senses.gloss: Confused and forgetful because of old age.
examples: He joked that he was going *senile*, but nobody laughed.
*Senile* dementia was the old name for the condition.
She seemed *more senile* each time we visited.

takes: *to* + noun — *senior to everyone else on the team*
contrast: After *senior* use *to*, never *than*: *She is senior to me*, not *senior than me*.

senses.gloss: Higher in rank, or longer in the job, than other people.
examples: She's a *senior* editor at the paper.
Two *more senior* officers reviewed the case.
He is *senior* to me by three years.

senses.gloss: Older; meant for older people.
examples: *Senior* citizens ride the city bus for free.
Ask about the *senior* discount before you pay.

senses.gloss: Of the last year of high school or college.
examples: My *senior* year was the best one.
The *senior* class voted to go to Chicago.
*Senior* prom is the third Friday in May.

contrast: A *sensational* dinner is wonderful; *sensational* reporting is cheap and shocking. The noun it goes with tells you which.

senses.gloss: Extremely good; wonderful.
examples: The food at that place is *sensational*.
She gave a *sensational* performance on opening night.

senses.gloss: Written or presented to shock and excite people.
examples: The paper ran a *sensational* headline about the mayor.
The trial got *more sensational* with every witness.
*Sensational* coverage of the crash upset the families.

senses.gloss: Using shocking stories and details to attract attention.
examples: The coverage was *sensationalistic* and thin on facts.
He hosts a *sensationalistic* talk show.
Local news has gotten *more sensationalistic* since the ratings dropped.

contrast: Not the opposite of *sensitive*. And the second meaning survives mostly in *knocked senseless* and *beaten senseless*.

senses.gloss: Having no purpose or meaning; stupid.
examples: The *senseless* killing shocked the whole town.
It was a *senseless* waste of money.
Arguing about it now is *senseless*.

senses.gloss: Unconscious.
examples: He was knocked *senseless* by the fall.
The blow left her *senseless* on the floor.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the senses — sight, hearing, touch, taste and smell.
examples: *Sensory* nerves carry signals to the brain.
The museum has a *sensory* room for small children.
*Sensory* overload hits me in big stores.

contrast: *Sensual* usually points to physical, often sexual pleasure; *sensuous* to pleasure the senses take in art, music or food.

senses.gloss: Connected with physical, often sexual pleasure.
examples: Her voice on the record is low and *sensual*.
They danced a slow, *sensual* tango.
The film is *more sensual* than the novel it came from.

contrast: Keep it apart from *sensual*: *sensuous* is about pleasure in colors, sounds and textures, with no sexual meaning attached.

senses.gloss: Giving pleasure to the senses.
examples: She loves the *sensuous* texture of velvet.
His poems are full of *sensuous* detail — smell, color, sound.
The soup was rich and *sensuous*.

senses.gloss: Able to feel and be aware of things.
examples: Whales are *sentient* beings.
The movie asks whether the robot is *sentient*.
The law protects *sentient* animals from cruelty.

senses.gloss: Showing tender feelings, often more than the situation deserves.
examples: He gets *sentimental* after two beers.
The ending is *sentimental*, but I cried anyway.
She's *more sentimental* about the old house than I am.

senses.gloss: Valued for the memories attached to it, not for the money.
examples: The ring has *sentimental* value.
I keep the letters for *sentimental* reasons.

contrast: The adjective ends in a schwa — *SEP-ruht*; the verb is *SEP-uh-rayt*. Same spelling, two pronunciations.

senses.gloss: Not joined to, or not together with, something else.
examples: The kids have *separate* rooms now.
Keep the raw chicken *separate* from the salad.
We arrived in two *separate* cars.

senses.gloss: Different; not the same one.
examples: That's a *separate* question, and we'll get to it.
Her work life and her home life are completely *separate*.

contrast: *Separate* is a plain state — apart or different. *Separated* says something pulled them apart, and of a couple it means living apart but not yet divorced.

senses.gloss: No longer living together as a couple, but not divorced.
examples: They've been *separated* for about a year.
My parents are *separated*, not divorced.

senses.gloss: Kept apart from something or someone else.
examples: The twins were *separated* at birth.
The two wings of the school are *separated* by a courtyard.

senses.gloss: Wanting a region to break away and become its own country.
examples: A *separatist* movement grew in the north.
*Separatist* fighters took the airport.
He joined a small *separatist* party in his twenties.

contrast: A *septic tank* uses an older sense — bacteria break the waste down. Nothing there is infected.

senses.gloss: Infected with harmful bacteria.
examples: The wound turned *septic* within two days.
She was rushed in with *septic* shock.
An untreated cut like that can go *septic*.

senses.gloss: Following one after another in a fixed order.
examples: The files are stored in *sequential* order.
The tickets have *sequential* numbers.
The training is *sequential*: you can't skip a step.

senses.gloss: Covered with small shiny disks sewn onto the cloth.
examples: She wore a *sequined* dress to the party.
A *sequined* jacket caught the stage lights.
The costumes were heavily *sequined*.

senses.gloss: From Serbia, or having to do with Serbia and its language.
examples: *Serbian* is written in two alphabets.
We went to a *Serbian* film festival downtown.
Her husband is *Serbian*.

senses.gloss: Happening by luck, and turning out well.
examples: Our meeting was completely *serendipitous*.
It was a *serendipitous* discovery in the back of the archive.
Nothing is *more serendipitous* than finding the right book by accident.

senses.gloss: Completely calm and peaceful.
examples: She stayed *serene* through the whole hearing.
A *serene* lake at dawn is worth the early start.
The garden is *more serene* on a weekday morning.

contrast: Sounds exactly like *cereal*, the breakfast food — different word, same pronunciation.

senses.gloss: Doing the same thing again and again.
examples: Police were hunting a *serial* killer.
He's a *serial* entrepreneur — this is his fifth company.
She called him a *serial* liar to his face.

senses.gloss: Forming or belonging to a series.
examples: Write down the *serial* number on the back.
The novel first appeared in *serial* form.

senses.gloss: Having a row of small points along the edge, like a saw.
examples: Use a *serrated* knife for bread.
The leaves have *serrated* edges.
The blade is *serrated* near the handle.

senses.gloss: Good enough to do the job, though nothing special.
examples: His Spanish is *serviceable* — he can order dinner and ask directions.
The hotel was plain but *serviceable*.

senses.gloss: Still in working condition; usable.
examples: Only two of the trucks are still *serviceable*.
The old boots are *serviceable* for another winter.

senses.gloss: Too eager to obey and please, like a servant.
examples: His *servile* manner around the boss made everyone uncomfortable.
She refused to be *servile* to anyone.
The letter struck a *servile* tone that embarrassed the whole department.

position: both — the *ready* meaning only after a verb
comparison: not gradable — though *more set in his ways* is common
takes: *on* + *-ing*; *against* + noun — *set on leaving*, *set against the idea*
contrast: Mostly a verb and a noun. As an adjective it lives in a few patterns: *a set time*, *all set*, *set in his ways*, *set on going*.

senses.gloss: Fixed or arranged in advance.
examples: We meet at a *set* time every Monday.
The restaurant offers a *set* menu for thirty dollars.
There's no *set* rule about how long it takes.

senses.gloss: Ready.
examples: Are you all *set*?
We're *set* to leave at six.

senses.gloss: Determined about something, or unwilling to change.
examples: He's *set* in his ways and won't try anything new.
She's *set* on going to law school.
They were dead *set* against the plan.

senses.gloss: Living a regular life in one place.
examples: They finally feel *settled* in the new town.
Once the kids were *settled*, she went back to school.

senses.gloss: Calm and unlikely to change.
examples: The weather looks *settled* for the weekend.
The market is *settled* after a rough month.

senses.gloss: Very bad or serious.
examples: She's in *severe* pain.
The storm did *severe* damage to the pier.
This winter was *more severe* than last.

senses.gloss: Strict and harsh.
examples: The judge handed down a *severe* sentence.
He gave me a *severe* look over his glasses.

senses.gloss: Very plain, with no decoration.
examples: Her hair was pulled back in a *severe* bun.
The building's lines are *severe* and gray.

senses.gloss: Cut off, or cut completely through.
examples: Surgeons reattached the *severed* finger.
A *severed* cable left the whole block dark.
He still talks about those *severed* friendships.

senses.gloss: Treating one sex as less able or less important than the other.
examples: That joke was *sexist* and everyone knew it.
The dress code is openly *sexist*.
Ads from the fifties look *more sexist* every year.

contrast: A false friend: Russian *сексуальный* often means *sexy*. English *sexual* is the neutral, technical word — *a sexy dress*, never *a sexual dress*.

senses.gloss: Having to do with sex or physical attraction.
examples: *Sexual* attraction is not the same thing as love.
The novel deals with *sexual* relationships openly.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the two sexes, or with reproduction.
examples: *Sexual* equality at work is still a fight.
Most plants use *sexual* reproduction.

senses.gloss: Sexually attractive.
examples: He looked *sexy* in that jacket.
It's the *sexiest* song on the album.

senses.gloss: Informal: exciting and interesting to people.
examples: Budget reform is not a *sexy* topic.
They needed a *sexier* name for the product.

senses.gloss: Worn out and untidy from long use.
examples: He wore a *shabby* coat with a torn pocket.
The lobby looked *shabbier* than in the photos.

senses.gloss: Unfair and mean.
examples: That was *shabby* treatment after twenty years on the job.
It's a *shabby* way to treat a friend.

senses.gloss: Protected from direct sunlight.
examples: We found a *shaded* spot for the picnic.
The path is *shaded* most of the way up.
The *shaded* seats at the ballpark sell out first.

senses.gloss: Full of shadows and hard to see into.
examples: A *shadowy* corridor led down to the basement.
The room stays *shadowy* even at noon.

senses.gloss: Mysterious and secretive.
examples: A *shadowy* figure was standing by the gate.
The money came from a *shadowy* offshore fund.

senses.gloss: Sheltered from the sun; giving shade.
examples: We sat on a *shady* bench by the river.
The north side of the yard is *shadier*.

senses.gloss: Informal: probably dishonest.
examples: That deal sounds *shady* to me.
He made his money in some *shady* business out west.

senses.gloss: Covered with long, thick, untidy hair.
examples: A *shaggy* dog followed us all the way home.
His hair was long and *shaggy*.
The pony's coat gets *shaggier* every winter.

contrast: *Shaken* is how a person feels after a shock; *shaky* describes hands, a voice or anything unsteady.

senses.gloss: Upset and unsteady after a shock.
examples: She was badly *shaken* by the accident.
He looked *shaken* when he came out of the office.
The driver was *more shaken* than hurt.

senses.gloss: Trembling, and hard to control.
examples: My hands were *shaky* after the second coffee.
He answered in a *shaky* voice.

senses.gloss: Not firm or steady.
examples: Don't put the vase on that *shaky* table.
The ladder felt *shakier* the higher I went.

senses.gloss: Weak and not to be relied on.
examples: The evidence is *shaky* at best.
The team got off to a *shaky* start.

contrast: Almost always before a noun. The same word is a noun: *the whole trial was a sham*.

senses.gloss: Pretending to be real, and meant to fool people.
examples: The election was a *sham* vote with one candidate.
They were arrested over a *sham* marriage.
*Sham* charities take the money and disappear.

senses.gloss: Showing in your face that you are ashamed.
examples: He gave a *shamefaced* apology and sat down.
She looked *shamefaced* when the teacher read her note out loud.
The *shamefaced* players walked off the field.

contrast: *Shameful* describes the act; *ashamed* describes the person: *a shameful lie*, but *he felt ashamed*.

senses.gloss: So bad that the people responsible should be ashamed.
examples: It was a *shameful* way to end a long career.
Conditions in the camp are *shameful*.
Nothing was *more shameful* than the cover-up that followed.

senses.gloss: Doing something bad or embarrassing without any shame at all.
examples: That was a *shameless* plug for his own book.
*Shameless* lying got him through the interview.
She is *shameless* about asking for favors.

senses.gloss: Having no clear shape or form.
examples: She wore a *shapeless* gray sweater.
The clay was still a *shapeless* lump.
His argument was *shapeless* and hard to follow.

contrast: An adjective, though it ends in *-ly*: *shapely legs*, never *she walked shapely*.

senses.gloss: Having an attractive shape.
examples: The dancer had long, *shapely* legs.
A *shapely* vase stood on the mantel.
The hedge is *shapelier* since the gardener came.

senses.gloss: Used, owned or felt by two or more people.
examples: We have a *shared* bathroom down the hall.
A *shared* interest in old movies brought them together.
Their *shared* history makes every argument worse.

contrast: *Sharp* is also an adverb in time phrases — *at seven o'clock sharp* — and in music a *sharp* note is slightly too high.

senses.gloss: Having an edge or a point that cuts easily.
examples: Careful — that knife is *sharp*.
Use the *sharpest* scissors in the drawer.
He cut his hand on a *sharp* piece of metal.

senses.gloss: Sudden and large, of a change or a turn.
examples: There's a *sharp* turn at the bottom of the hill.
The city saw a *sharp* rise in rents.
Prices took a *sharp* drop in May.

senses.gloss: Quick to notice or understand things.
examples: She still has a *sharp* mind at ninety.
His *sharp* eyes caught the typo on page one.
He's *sharper* than anyone else in the room.

senses.gloss: Sudden and severe, of a pain.
examples: I felt a *sharp* pain in my side.
A *sharp* stab of cold air hit us at the door.

senses.gloss: Harsh and critical.
examples: Her tone got *sharp* toward the end.
There was a *sharp* exchange at the school board meeting.

senses.gloss: Strong and slightly bitter, of a taste or smell.
examples: The recipe calls for *sharp* cheddar.
The wine has a *sharp* finish.

senses.gloss: Good at noticing small details.
examples: A *sharp-eyed* reader spotted the error.
You have to be *sharp-eyed* to find the bird in that photo.
A *more sharp-eyed* editor would have caught it.

contrast: In British English *shattered* also means exhausted. Americans say *wiped out* for that.

senses.gloss: Broken into many small pieces.
examples: *Shattered* glass covered the sidewalk.
He swept up the *shattered* plate.

senses.gloss: Deeply upset, with your life or hopes broken.
examples: She was *shattered* by the news.
The family is still *shattered* a year later.

senses.gloss: So shocking or destructive that it breaks something apart.
examples: The verdict was a *shattering* blow to the family.
*Shattering* news came late that night.
There was a *shattering* crash from the kitchen.

senses.gloss: Made so that it will not break into pieces.
examples: The lenses in these glasses are *shatterproof*.
*Shatterproof* glass keeps the kids safe.
We bought *shatterproof* ornaments after the cat arrived.

senses.gloss: With the hair cut off close to the skin.
examples: He has a *shaved* head and a gray beard.
Her legs were freshly *shaved*.

senses.gloss: Cut into very thin slices.
examples: *Shaved* ice with syrup is summer around here.
The salad comes with *shaved* Parmesan on top.

senses.gloss: Embarrassed because you have done something silly or wrong.
examples: He gave me a *sheepish* grin and apologized.
She looked *sheepish* about forgetting my birthday.
The *sheepish* look on his face said everything.

contrast: In *hard-shelled* and *soft-shelled* the word means the opposite — having a shell of that kind.

senses.gloss: With the shell taken off.
examples: The recipe calls for a cup of *shelled* walnuts.
Buy *shelled* pistachios if you're in a hurry.
*Shelled* peas cook in five minutes.

senses.gloss: Protected from wind, rain or sun.
examples: We ate lunch in a *sheltered* corner of the yard.
The bay is *sheltered* from the north wind.

senses.gloss: Kept away from anything difficult or unpleasant in life.
examples: She had a *sheltered* childhood in a small town.
He's led a *more sheltered* life than he admits.

senses.gloss: Constantly moving or changing.
examples: *Shifting* sands buried the road overnight.
The *shifting* politics of the region make planning hard.
Their *shifting* stories made the police suspicious.

form: -less from an old sense of *shift*, meaning effort

senses.gloss: Lazy, with no ambition to do anything.
examples: He called his nephew *shiftless* and lazy.
A *shiftless* crew showed up an hour late.
The main character is a *shiftless* dreamer who finishes nothing.

senses.gloss: Looking or sounding dishonest.
examples: He had *shifty* eyes and a nervous laugh.
The salesman seemed *shifty* from the first minute.
The longer he talked, the *shiftier* he sounded.

senses.gloss: Shining with a soft, moving light.
examples: She wore a *shimmery* blue dress.
The lake looked *shimmery* in the heat.
This eyeshadow is *more shimmery* than I expected.

position: both — the *excellent* meaning only before a noun
contrast: *Shining* often carries approval — *a shining example*. *Shiny* only describes a surface: *shiny shoes*.

senses.gloss: Giving out or reflecting light.
examples: Her eyes were *shining* with tears.
A *shining* moon lit the whole road.

senses.gloss: Excellent; standing out from everything around it.
examples: She's a *shining* example of how to do this job.
That was the one *shining* moment of the season.

senses.gloss: Smooth and bright, reflecting the light.
examples: His shoes were black and *shiny*.
The new coin is *shinier* than the old one.
Kids grab whatever is *shiniest* on the shelf.

senses.gloss: Happening or used on a ship.
examples: They met during a *shipboard* romance.
*Shipboard* life takes some getting used to.
The crew ran *shipboard* drills every morning.

senses.gloss: Neat, clean and in good order.
examples: The garage is finally *shipshape*.
She left the kitchen *shipshape*.
Everything on deck was *shipshape* before we sailed.

contrast: Vulgar. Fine among friends, never at work or in writing — use *lousy* or *crummy* there.

senses.gloss: Very bad, or very unkind.
examples: We had a *shitty* week.
That was a *shitty* thing to say to her.
The second hotel was even *shittier* than the first.

senses.gloss: Badly made or badly done.
examples: They used *shoddy* materials and the roof leaked by spring.
The second contractor's work was even *shoddier*.

senses.gloss: Unfair and dishonest.
examples: That's *shoddy* treatment of a loyal customer.
He gave a *shoddy* excuse for breaking his promise.

senses.gloss: Wearing no shoes.
examples: *Shoeless* kids ran across the hot sand.
He answered the door *shoeless* and half asleep.
Guests arrive *shoeless* and leave their boots by the door.

senses.gloss: Dirty or damaged from sitting on display in a store.
examples: The last box was *shopworn* and marked down.
They sell *shopworn* furniture at half price.

senses.gloss: No longer fresh or original.
examples: The speech was full of *shopworn* phrases.
That argument is *shopworn* by now.

senses.gloss: Cut very short, of hair or wool.
examples: A *shorn* sheep looks half its size.
His *shorn* head made him look ten years younger.

senses.gloss: Stripped of something you used to have.
examples: The king was left *shorn* of all real power.
The bill passed *shorn* of its best provisions.

senses.gloss: Having short hair or short fur.
examples: A *short-haired* terrier is easier to groom.
She's been *short-haired* since college.
*Short-haired* breeds shed less in the house.

contrast: In hockey a team is *short-handed* while a player sits in the penalty box. At an office, *short-staffed* is the everyday word.

senses.gloss: Without enough people to do the work.
examples: We're *short-handed* tonight, so expect a wait.
The kitchen has been *short-handed* all month.
They played *short-handed* for two minutes.

contrast: Two pronunciations are standard in the US: *short-LYVD* and *short-LIVD*.

senses.gloss: Lasting only a short time.
examples: Their happiness was *short-lived*.
It was a *short-lived* TV show from the nineties.
The truce proved *short-lived*.

senses.gloss: Of simple food cooked quickly to order in a diner.
examples: He worked as a *short-order* cook for years.
The diner has a *short-order* menu — eggs, burgers, fries.
*Short-order* cooking is all speed and timing.

senses.gloss: Reaching only a short distance, or covering only the near future.
examples: *Short-range* missiles were moved to the border.
The forecast is only a *short-range* guess.
We made *short-range* plans and left the rest open.

contrast: As an adverb phrase it splits and drops the hyphen: *in the short run*.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the near future only.
examples: *Short-run* profits look good, but the debt keeps growing.
The tax cut is a *short-run* fix.
*Short-run* costs rose while output fell.

senses.gloss: Without enough employees.
examples: The clinic is badly *short-staffed*.
We've been *short-staffed* since two nurses quit.
A *short-staffed* ER means long waits.

senses.gloss: Quick to get angry.
examples: He's *short-tempered* before his first coffee.
A *short-tempered* boss keeps everyone quiet.
She gets *more short-tempered* when she's tired.

contrast: For the eye condition Americans normally say *nearsighted*; in the US *shortsighted* usually means bad planning.

senses.gloss: Not thinking about what will happen later.
examples: Cutting the training budget is *shortsighted*.
It was a *shortsighted* decision that cost them the contract.
Nothing is *more shortsighted* than ignoring the repairs.

senses.gloss: Unable to see distant things clearly.
examples: He's *shortsighted* and can't read the board without glasses.
She's been *shortsighted* since grade school.

senses.gloss: Attracting attention, often too much of it.
examples: The ring is a little *showy* for the office.
*Showy* red flowers fill the front bed.
His second car is even *showier* than the first.

senses.gloss: Cut or torn into thin strips.
examples: Add a cup of *shredded* cheese on top.
*Shredded* documents filled three garbage bags.
The lettuce comes *shredded* in a bag.

senses.gloss: Good at judging people and situations, and at using that to your advantage.
examples: She's a *shrewd* negotiator.
That was a *shrewd* guess.
He's *shrewder* about money than his brother.

senses.gloss: High and unpleasantly loud.
examples: A *shrill* whistle cut through the noise.
Her voice got *shriller* as she got angrier.

senses.gloss: Loud and angry in a way that stops people listening.
examples: The debate turned *shrill* within ten minutes.
*Shrill* attacks from both sides drowned out the facts.
